items.title: Arpit Bhayani: px0 is now a complete AI-coding-review workbench — AI-driven rebase conflicts and commit messages
items.summary: px0.ai's latest release turns `px0` (no args) into a full workbench: open any repo or PR, spin up separate instances per workspace, trigger "Rebase with AI" to resolve merge conflicts using your local coding harness, and ask AI to rewrite a commit message right from the squash/merge dialog. Now also supports GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo and Bitbucket, not just GitHub.
items.why: Reviewing and merging AI-generated code is turning into its own bottleneck — this folds the annoying parts (conflict resolution, commit hygiene) into the same AI workflow instead of kicking you back to a plain git CLI.
items.action: If you already use px0.ai, run `px0 --update` and try "Rebase with AI" on your next messy merge; if not, `px0` with no args is the fastest way to see the new workbench.

items.title: Paul Iusztin: stop tuning how agents reason — define what they're reasoning about instead
items.summary: Pairs Jev (a decision model) with an explicit ontology: instead of asking an LLM to reason through every case, you define the possible outcomes and relations in code, Jev classifies against them with a confidence score, and the agent routes by that score — high confidence executes, medium escalates to an LLM, low goes to a human. A commenter from Visa reports applying the same pattern to support-ticket escalations dropped them ~40%.
items.why: A badly-defined decision space will make even a great model guess wrong with high confidence — this makes that failure mode visible and auditable instead of invisible inside a prompt.
items.action: Next agent step that currently asks an LLM to pick from a fixed set of outcomes, write that outcome set down as an explicit ontology first, then gate execution on a confidence threshold.

items.title: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, the production inference framework powering DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
items.summary: DeepSeek released DeepInfer (Apache-2.0, github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer) today: the same high-throughput, low-latency inference stack it runs in production, shared so others can lower compute costs and energy use when self-hosting DeepSeek models. Surfaced via @swyx's retweet of the first-party announcement (2.4M views).

items.action: If you're self-hosting any DeepSeek model, worth a spin to see how DeepInfer compares to your current vLLM/TGI setup on throughput and cost.

items.title: DeepLearning.AI + Chroma launch a new "Context Engineering" course
items.summary: Announced today: an intermediate course by Jeff Huber (Chroma CEO) and Drew Breunig (editor, O'Reilly's Context Engineering Handbook) on giving agents the right information, in the right format, at the right time — agentic search, context pruning/compaction/scratchpads, and agentic memory, building agent harnesses in Python from scratch and measuring improvements with traces and evals.
items.why: This is the exact problem underneath most "my agent forgot/misused context" bugs, taught by the people literally writing the handbook on it.
items.action: Worth at least the first module on context pruning/compaction — it maps directly onto harness and memory design, not just prompting.

items.title: Cole Medin: let your AI agent do its own harness engineering
items.summary: Posted today. Shows a two-loop system for production agents (not just coding agents): one loop turns escalations into private, per-user memory; the other uses LangSmith Engine to propose rule/skill changes from traces, with versioning, rollback and Slack approval so a human stays in the loop. Built on LangChain's Managed Deep Agents. Flagged "includes paid promotion" — judged acceptable since the sponsor's product is the actual technical subject of the video, not a separate ad segment. Summarized from the chapter list and description; TubeAlfred transcript tool was unavailable this run (disclosed fallback).
items.why: This is the same "harness that improves itself" idea coding agents use, applied to any production agent — with the actual approval/rollback mechanics, not just the concept.
items.action: 16 minutes. The live demo (7:48–11:34) is the part worth not skipping if you only have time for one section.

items.title: Al Chen (Cisco): shipping AI into 5 major banks without a 12-month compliance wait
items.summary: A war story on what it actually takes to get AI software through bank security/compliance review: the build pipeline, agents writing and testing their own CVE-remediation exploits, backup/restore verification, PII leaking through LLM-as-judge setups, and why zero data leakage and data sovereignty are never free. No sponsor flag. A top comment pushes back usefully on whether LLM-as-judge is really safer than rigid pattern matching for PII/PCI scrubbing.
items.why: Most "AI in the enterprise" content stays at the pilot stage — this is what the actual security/compliance gate looks like once you try to ship past it.
items.action: 18 minutes, including the PII-via-LLM-judge segment that's most directly relevant if you're building any agent that touches regulated data.
